claim: Mass transport limitations (nutrients, oxygen, waste diffusion) of macroscale 3D tissue culture are circumvented by initially culturing murine or porcine adipocytes in 2D.
source: Mass transport limitations (nutrients, oxygen, waste diffusion) of macroscale 3D tissue culture are circumvented by initially culturing murine or porcine adipocytes in 2D, after which bulk fat tissue is produced by mechanically harvesting and aggregating the lipid-filled adipocytes into 3D constructs using alginate or transglutaminase binders.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach used to overcome mass transport limitations.

claim: Bulk fat tissue is produced by mechanically harvesting and aggregating lipid-filled adipocytes into 3D constructs using alginate or transglutaminase binders.
source: Mass transport limitations (nutrients, oxygen, waste diffusion) of macroscale 3D tissue culture are circumvented by initially culturing murine or porcine adipocytes in 2D, after which bulk fat tissue is produced by mechanically harvesting and aggregating the lipid-filled adipocytes into 3D constructs using alginate or transglutaminase binders.
evidence: The manuscript describes the method used to produce bulk fat tissue.

claim: The 3D fat tissues were visually similar to fat tissue harvested from animals.
source: The 3D fat tissues were visually similar to fat tissue harvested from animals, with matching textures based on uniaxial compression tests.
evidence: The manuscript reports visual similarity based on observation.

claim: The 3D fat tissues had matching textures to animal fat tissue based on uniaxial compression tests.
source: The 3D fat tissues were visually similar to fat tissue harvested from animals, with matching textures based on uniaxial compression tests.
evidence: The manuscript reports mechanical testing data comparing cultured and native fat tissues.

claim: The mechanical properties of cultured fat tissues were based on binder choice and concentration.
source: The mechanical properties of cultured fat tissues were based on binder choice and concentration, and changes in the fatty acid compositions of cellular triacylglyceride and phospholipids were observed after lipid supplementation (soybean oil) during in vitro culture.
evidence: The manuscript reports mechanical testing data showing differences based on binder type and concentration.

claim: Changes in the fatty acid compositions of cellular triacylglyceride and phospholipids were observed after lipid supplementation (soybean oil) during in vitro culture.
source: The mechanical properties of cultured fat tissues were based on binder choice and concentration, and changes in the fatty acid compositions of cellular triacylglyceride and phospholipids were observed after lipid supplementation (soybean oil) during in vitro culture.
evidence: The manuscript reports lipidomics data showing changes in fatty acid composition with Intralipid supplementation.

claim: Fat is key to the taste and texture of meat.
source: However, fat is key to the taste and texture of meat (He et al., 2020; Moritz et al., 2015; Frank et al., 2016; Frank et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Peak evaluation scores were achieved with beef samples containing ~36% crude fat.
source: For example, peak evaluation scores were achieved with beef samples containing ~36% crude fat (Iida et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Hundreds of volatile compounds are released when meat is cooked, with a majority originating from lipids.
source: Hundreds of volatile compounds are released when meat is cooked, with a majority originating from lipids (Frank et al., 2017; Ba et al., 2012; Mottram et al., 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Fat is responsible for the species-specific flavor of meat.
source: Fat is also responsible for the species-specific flavor of meat, making it important for reproducing the flavors of specific animals (Ramalingam et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In vitro-grown fat could be used to enhance existing plant-based meats.
source: In addition to cultivated meat, in vitro-grown fat could also be used to enhance existing plant-based meats, as complex species-specific flavors of animals are difficult to recapitulate de novo (Fish et al., 2020; van Vliet et al., 2021; Bohrer, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and represents a potential application.

claim: Complex species-specific flavors of animals are difficult to recapitulate de novo in plant-based meats.
source: In addition to cultivated meat, in vitro-grown fat could also be used to enhance existing plant-based meats, as complex species-specific flavors of animals are difficult to recapitulate de novo (Fish et al., 2020; van Vliet et al., 2021; Bohrer, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Producing macroscale tissues remains a major challenge due to mass transport limitations.
source: While cultured fat stands to greatly improve the quality of alternative proteins, producing macroscale tissues remains a major challenge due to mass transport limitations.
evidence: The claim is supported by established knowledge in tissue engineering.

claim: Oxygen and nutrients are only able to diffuse through several hundred microns of dense tissue.
source: Even millimeter-scale in vitro tissues are challenging to generate, as oxygen and nutrients are only able to diffuse through several hundred microns of dense tissue (Coyle et al., 2019; Murphy et al., 2017; Helmlinger et al., 1997; Jain et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: All tissues must remain within several hundred microns of a perfusion channel.
source: A dense array is required when incorporating perfusion channels, as all tissues must remain within several hundred microns of a channel (Yamamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Lipid accumulation decreases considerably once cells are ~1 mm away from a perfusion channel in adipose tissue.
source: For adipose tissue, lipid accumulation decreases considerably once cells are ~1 mm away from a perfusion channel (Li et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Spontaneous vessel formation may not be feasible for centimeter- to meter-scale tissues, as cultivated cells may die during the time required for the vasculature to form.
source: However, spontaneous vessel formation may not be feasible for centimeter- to meter-scale tissues, as cultivated cells may die during the time required for the vasculature to form (Unal et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Capillaries may be too small to deliver a sufficient volume of media when supporting larger tissues.
source: Capillaries may also be too small to deliver a sufficient volume of media when supporting larger tissues (Tetzlaff and Fischer, 2018; Moya et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Adipose tissue in vivo is a dense aggregation of lipid-filled adipocytes with a sparse extracellular matrix.
source: We hypothesized that aggregating individual adipocytes would be sufficient to reproduce the taste, nutrition, and texture profile of fat, as adipose tissue in vivo is a dense aggregation of lipid-filled adipocytes with a sparse extracellular matrix (ECM) (Mescher, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: At day 15, cultured adipocytes were 81.6% (±5.5%) positive for peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ).
source: At day 15, cultured adipocytes were 81.6% (±5.5%) positive for peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ) (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 30-day adipocytes contained ~3 times more lipid per cell than 15-day adipocytes.
source: 30-day adipocytes contained ~3 times more lipid per cell than 15-day adipocytes (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A positive correlation was observed between adipogenic culture duration and lipid droplet size.
source: A positive correlation was observed between adipogenic culture duration and lipid droplet size (Figure 2E, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipid droplet diameter distribution data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mean lipid droplet diameters for 15- and 30-day adipocytes were 8.1 µm (±0.04 SEM) and 11.1 µm (±0.1 SEM), respectively.
source: Mean lipid droplet diameters for 15- and 30-day adipocytes were 8.1 µm (±0.04 SEM) and 11.1 µm (±0.1 SEM), respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of lipid droplet sizes.

claim: Cultured adipocytes exhibited the appearance of packed lipid droplets observed when imaging native adipocytes from various animals, particularly that of 7-day old mouse (7D mouse) and chicken.
source: Cultured adipocytes exhibited the appearance of packed lipid droplets observed when imaging native adipocytes from various animals, particularly that of 7-day old mouse (7D mouse) and chicken (Figure 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual comparison in Figure 2F.

claim: One culture flask with 175 cm2 surface area generally yielded ~0.8 g of cell-scraped adipocytes.
source: We found that one culture flask with 175 cm2 surface area generally yielded ~0.8 g of cell-scraped adipocytes (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: Sodium alginate and microbial transglutaminase (mTG) as 'generally recognized as safe' (GRAS) materials in the United States were selected as binders for cultured adipocytes.
source: Sodium alginate and microbial transglutaminase (mTG) as 'generally recognized as safe' (GRAS) materials in the United States were selected as binders for cultured adipocytes, with precedent for alginate as a fat replacer and mTG as a binder in meat products (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; ECFR, 1982; FDA, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to regulatory documents.

claim: Alginate fat tissues containing 15- and 30-day adipocytes exhibited mean compressive stresses of 11.1 kPa (±5.2) and 12.8 kPa (±7.3) at 50% strain respectively.
source: Alginate fat tissues containing 15- and 30-day adipocytes exhibited mean compressive stresses of 11.1 kPa (±5.2) and 12.8 kPa (±7.3) at 50% strain respectively (p=0.7304, Welch's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by mechanical testing data.

claim: For 15- and 30-day mTG-based cultured fat tissues, the mean resistances to compression were 0.5 kPa (±0.2) and 0.7 kPa (±0.2) at 50% strain, respectively.
source: For 15- and 30-day mTG-based cultured fat tissues, the mean resistances to compression were 0.5 kPa (±0.2) and 0.7 kPa (±0.2) at 50% strain, respectively (p=0.1030, Welch's t-test).
evidence: The claim is supported by mechanical testing data.

claim: At 50% strain, mean compressive stresses for beef and pork fat tissues were 20.2 kPa (±12.5) and 35.6 kPa (±17.5), respectively.
source: At 50% strain, mean compressive stresses for beef and pork fat tissues were 20.2 kPa (±12.5) and 35.6 kPa (±17.5), respectively, while the mean value for chicken fat tissue was 6.2 kPa (±2.0).
evidence: The claim is supported by mechanical testing data.

claim: The mean compressive stress for chicken fat tissue at 50% strain was 6.2 kPa (±2.0).
source: At 50% strain, mean compressive stresses for beef and pork fat tissues were 20.2 kPa (±12.5) and 35.6 kPa (±17.5), respectively, while the mean value for chicken fat tissue was 6.2 kPa (±2.0).
evidence: The claim is supported by mechanical testing data.

claim: Lard and tallow samples had mean compressive stresses of 4.6 kPa (±1.4) and 2.5 kPa (±0.9) at 50% strain, respectively.
source: mTG-based cultured fat tissues were more similar to rendered fats, although lard and tallow samples appeared stronger with mean compressive stresses of 4.6 kPa (±1.4) and 2.5 kPa (±0.9) at 50% strain, respectively (Figure 3F, ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by mechanical testing data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: mTG fat tissues maintained some resistance during unloading, while rendered fats did not rebound after compression.
source: mTG fat tissues maintained some resistance during unloading, while rendered fats did not rebound after compression.
evidence: The claim is based on mechanical testing observations.

claim: Lipid supplementation has been reported to enhance adipogenic differentiation.
source: Lipid supplementation (e.g., with Intralipid) has been reported to enhance adipogenic differentiation and may thus be a useful strategy in enhancing fat cell lipid accumulation during cultured fat production (El Hadri et al., 2004; Ding et al., 2003; Kokta et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2015; Yanting et al., 2018; Malodobra-Mazur et al., 2019; Jurek et al., 2020; Kim et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Unsupplemented IVFs contained significantly less 18:1 and 18:2 versus 7D and 67D mouse fats.
source: Unsupplemented IVFs contained significantly less 18:1 and 18:2 versus 7D and 67D mouse fats, as well as slightly less 18:0 and 18:3 than 67D mouse.
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomics data comparing fatty acid compositions.

claim: The addition of lipids (500–1000 µg/ml Intralipid) during cell culture altered adipocyte TAGs dose dependently.
source: The addition of lipids (500–1000 µg/ml Intralipid) during cell culture altered adipocyte TAGs dose dependently, generally bringing FA compositions closer to that of the native fats largely through a reduction in 16:1 and increase in 18:1.
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomics data showing dose-dependent changes.

claim: Intralipid-treated IVFs had elevated levels of 16:0 and 18 carbon FAs (18:0, 18:1, 18:2, 18:3), which correlates with the composition of soybean oil.
source: Intralipid-treated IVFs had elevated levels of 16:0 and 18 carbon FAs (18:0, 18:1, 18:2, 18:3), which correlates with the composition of soybean oil, the major constituent of Intralipid (aside from water) (Supplementary file 3; Abdelghany et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomics data and a citation about soybean oil composition.

claim: The increase in 18:3 in lipid supplemented adipocytes may reflect the uptake of alpha-linoleic acid from the Intralipid.
source: Notably, the increase in 18:3 in lipid supplemented adipocytes may reflect the uptake of alpha-linoleic acid from the Intralipid (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from lipidomics data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Unsupplemented IVFs contained low levels (2.9%±0.1) of polyunsaturated FAs (PUFAs).
source: Unsupplemented IVFs contained low levels (2.9%±0.1) of polyunsaturated FAs (PUFAs), but this increased to 12.3% (±2.7) with 1000 µg/ml of Intralipid, similar to that of 7D mouse.
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomics data.

claim: PUFA levels increased to 12.3% (±2.7) with 1000 µg/ml of Intralipid, similar to that of 7D mouse.
source: Unsupplemented IVFs contained low levels (2.9%±0.1) of polyunsaturated FAs (PUFAs), but this increased to 12.3% (±2.7) with 1000 µg/ml of Intralipid, similar to that of 7D mouse.
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomics data.

claim: Saturated FAs decreased from 48.2% (±0.9, unsupplemented IVFs) to 39.9% (±3.0, 1000 µg/ml Intralipid).
source: PUFA increases for Intralipid IVFs were mirrored by a decrease in saturated FAs (SFAs), going from 48.2% (±0.9, unsupplemented IVFs) to 39.9% (±3.0, 1000 µg/ml Intralipid).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomics data.

claim: Phospholipids have been reported to contribute significantly to meat flavor.
source: As phospholipids have been reported to contribute significantly to meat flavor, we additionally looked at IVF phospholipid FAs (Mottram and Edwards, 1983; Huang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Sample groups cultured in adipogenic media with 2% FBS contained over 2× fewer cells, yet had over 2× the lipid accumulation, versus groups with 20% FBS.
source: Interestingly, sample groups cultured in adipogenic media with 2% FBS contained over 2× fewer cells, yet had over 2× the lipid accumulation, versus groups with 20% FBS (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Lipids within cultured porcine adipocytes were multilocular, unlike native adipose from food animals (pig, chicken, cow).
source: When compared to native adipose from food animals (pig, chicken, cow), lipids within cultured porcine adipocytes were multilocular, unlike native adipose from food animals (pig, chicken, cow) (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy images shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In vitro and native porcine fats exhibited more similar FA profiles than murine cells, especially within the TAG fractions.
source: Unlike 3T3-L1s, in vitro and native porcine fats exhibited more similar FA profiles, especially within the TAG fractions (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The only major difference observed between in vitro and native porcine fat samples was a lack of 20:4 (>10% difference) in the phospholipids.
source: The only major difference observed between in vitro and native fat samples was a lack of 20:4 (>10% difference) in the phospholipids, with smaller differences observed for 18:0, 18:1, 16:0, also within the phospholipid fraction.
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomics data comparing in vitro and native porcine fats.

claim: Extended 2D culture (30 days) of in vitro adipocytes resulted in the emergence of larger lipid droplets, a key trait of white adipose tissue.
source: Here, we show that extended 2D culture (30 days) of in vitro adipocytes resulted in the emergence of larger lipid droplets, a key trait of white adipose tissue.
evidence: The claim is supported by lipid droplet size data.

claim: Enhanced adipogenesis in low serum or serum-free media has been reported by numerous groups.
source: Enhanced adipogenesis in low serum or serum-free media has been reported by numerous groups; the diminished lipid accumulation found in adipocytes differentiated in high serum conditions (e.g., 20% in this study) may be due to factors in FBS, such as transforming growth factor β, that have been found to be pro-proliferative and anti-adipogenic (Jurek et al., 2020; Mitić et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2012; Entenmann and Hauner, 1996; Sandhu et al., 2017; Sprenger et al., 2021; Boone et al., 2000; Suryawan and Hu, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The diminished lipid accumulation found in adipocytes differentiated in high serum conditions may be due to factors in FBS, such as transforming growth factor β, that have been found to be pro-proliferative and anti-adipogenic.
source: Enhanced adipogenesis in low serum or serum-free media has been reported by numerous groups; the diminished lipid accumulation found in adipocytes differentiated in high serum conditions (e.g., 20% in this study) may be due to factors in FBS, such as transforming growth factor β, that have been found to be pro-proliferative and anti-adipogenic (Jurek et al., 2020; Mitić et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2012; Entenmann and Hauner, 1996; Sandhu et al., 2017; Sprenger et al., 2021; Boone et al., 2000; Suryawan and Hu, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature and inference from experimental data.

claim: Yorkshire pigs reportedly have no brown adipose tissue due to the lack of a functional UCP1 gene.
source: However, the lipid morphology observed in the Yorkshire pig DFAT cells of this study likely represents an immature white adipocyte phenotype, as Yorkshire pigs reportedly have no brown adipose tissue (due to the lack of a functional UCP1 gene) (Zheng et al., 2017; Berg et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Intralipid supplementation drastically increased porcine cell adipogenesis.
source: For example, in this study we found that Intralipid supplementation drastically increased porcine cell adipogenesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: DFAT cells have been shown to accumulate more intracellular lipids than adipose-derived stromal vascular cells.
source: Additionally, DFAT cells have been shown to accumulate more intracellular lipids than adipose-derived stromal vascular cells, making them a better choice for large-scale cultured fat production (Peng et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: mTG has been shown to greatly strengthen protein-rich materials.
source: As mTG has been shown to greatly strengthen protein-rich materials, the weaker mTG fat tissues may be due to a lack of extracellular protein available for crosslinking among the aggregated in vitro adipocytes (Broderick et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The weaker mTG fat tissues may be due to a lack of extracellular protein available for crosslinking among the aggregated in vitro adipocytes.
source: As mTG has been shown to greatly strengthen protein-rich materials, the weaker mTG fat tissues may be due to a lack of extracellular protein available for crosslinking among the aggregated in vitro adipocytes (Broderick et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from mechanical testing data and knowledge about mTG.

claim: ECM-promoting culture media components like ascorbic acid have been shown to improve in vitro adipogenesis.
source: It would also be interesting to investigate whether upregulating ECM deposition would improve mTG crosslinking, especially since ECM-promoting culture media components like ascorbic acid have also been shown to improve in vitro adipogenesis (Jurek et al., 2020; Cuaranta-Monroy et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2013; Thorrez et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Rodents lacking dietary oleic acid (18:1 ω-9) compensated with higher levels of 16:1, as endogenous production of oleic acid is insufficient to achieve the amounts typically found in normal tissue.
source: It has been shown that rodents lacking dietary oleic acid (18:1 ω-9) compensated with higher levels of 16:1, as endogenous production of oleic acid is insufficient to achieve the amounts typically found in normal tissue (Bourre et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The scarce presence of 18:2 for both murine and porcine cells is likely due an inability for mammals to synthesize linoleic acid (18:2 ω-6).
source: The scarce presence of 18:2 for both murine and porcine cells is likely due an inability for mammals to synthesize linoleic acid (18:2 ω-6), which may highlight the importance of its supplementation during in vitro culture (Hansen, 1986; Malcicka et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from lipidomics data and citations about mammalian fatty acid synthesis.

claim: Intralipid contains 44–62% linoleic acid.
source: Indeed, Intralipid treatment (44–62% linoleic acid) enriched 18:2 and raised overall PUFA levels for all in vitro adipocytes, with murine cells additionally achieving more similarity to native mouse fats in terms of 16:1 and 18:1 levels (Abdelghany et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation about Intralipid composition.

claim: The increase in 18:3 from Intralipid across murine and porcine adipocytes represents a potential enrichment in omega 3 PUFAs, as 18:3 in soybean oil is alpha-linoleic acid.
source: The increase in 18:3 from Intralipid across murine and porcine adipocytes represents a potential enrichment in omega 3 PUFAs, as 18:3 in soybean oil is alpha-linoleic acid.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from lipidomics data and knowledge about soybean oil composition.

claim: 20:4 levels in porcine IVFs were not uncommonly low, achieving the same value as reported elsewhere for pig fat (1.4% of all FAs).
source: 20:4 levels in porcine IVFs were not uncommonly low though, achieving the same value as reported elsewhere for pig fat (1.4% of all FAs) (Dinh et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: High 20:4 in native pig samples could be related to how native pork fat FAs are very pliable based on the animal's diet.
source: High 20:4 in our native pig samples could be related to how native pork fat FAs are very pliable based on the animal's diet (Wood et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is based on inference and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Arachidonic acid has been linked with both inflammation and enhanced meat flavor.
source: Ultimately, optimal intracellular 20:4 levels are unclear, as arachidonic acid has been linked with both inflammation and enhanced meat flavor (Calder, 2006; Adam et al., 2003; Takahashi, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Different strains of mice can have varying phospholipid compositions when fed the same diet.
source: It has been reported that different strains of mice can have varying phospholipid compositions when fed the same diet (Hulbert et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Aggregating in vitro adipocytes to generate cell-cultured animal fat using various binders unlocks a simplified approach of producing bulk cultured fat tissue with lower costs and direct scalability.
source: Aggregating in vitro adipocytes to generate cell-cultured animal fat using various binders unlocks a simplified approach of producing bulk cultured fat tissue with lower costs and direct scalability, addressing a key obstacle in cultivated meat production and contributing to the paradigm of food production using cell culture techniques.
evidence: The claim is based on the overall findings and implications of the study.

claim: The adipocyte aggregation approach is cell type and species agnostic.
source: The adipocyte aggregation approach is cell type and species agnostic, as demonstrated via the 3T3-L1s (adipogenic fibroblasts) and primary porcine DFAT cells (mesenchymal stem cell-like cells) in this study.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data using different cell types.

claim: Incorporating cultured fats or fat tissues into plant-based meats permits the creation of hybrid products, where sustainable and low-cost plant ingredients are enhanced by the complex species-specific flavors that arise from added animal fat cells.
source: Incorporating cultured fats or fat tissues into plant-based meats permits the creation of hybrid products, where sustainable and low-cost plant ingredients are enhanced by the complex species-specific flavors that arise from added animal fat cells.
evidence: The claim represents a potential application based on the study's findings.

claim: Cultivated meat may be more sustainable than conventional meat production.
source: Taken together, these approaches offer a potential path to producing meat (or realistic meat alternatives) without animal slaughter, while potentially being more sustainable than conventional meat production (Tuomisto et al., 2014; Tuomisto and de Mattos, 2011; Sun et al., 2015; Mattick et al., 2015; Odegard and Sinke, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature on sustainability.

claim: The degree of adipocyte lipid accumulation (cultured fat tissues produced using 15- versus 30-day-old adipocytes) did not have a significant impact on resistance to compression.
source: The degree of adipocyte lipid accumulation (cultured fat tissues produced using 15- versus 30-day-old adipocytes) did not have a significant impact on resistance to compression (Figure 3Ei, Fi).
evidence: The claim is supported by mechanical testing data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: The stress-strain profile of alginate-based cultured fat tissues were within the general range of livestock and poultry fat tissues.
source: The stress-strain profile of alginate-based cultured fat tissues were within the general range of livestock and poultry fat tissues, while displaying similar hysteresis behavior during loading and unloading (Figure 3E, ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by mechanical testing data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: During cell scraping, cultured adipocytes aggregated by the mechanical action of the cell scraper appeared like fat tissue or lipoaspirate.
source: During cell harvest, cultured adipocytes aggregated by the mechanical action of the cell scraper appeared like fat tissue or lipoaspirate (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and Video 2.

claim: Gentle treatment of the cells during culture media changes was key to preventing lift-off of lipid-filled adipocytes.
source: During cell culture, gentle treatment of the cells (e.g., when changing culture media) was key to preventing lift-off of lipid-filled adipocytes (detailed technique outlined in Video 1 and the Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations during cell culture.

claim: Adipocytes were scraped mechanically due to insufficient detachment when using Accumax.
source: Adipocytes were scraped mechanically due to insufficient detachment when using Accumax (incubation time: >20 min, data not shown).
evidence: The claim is based on experimental observations.

claim: Most studies that investigate 3T3-L1 adipogenesis in 2D are of limited culture duration (≤15 days), with lipid accumulation manifesting as small lipid droplets.
source: Most studies that investigate 3T3-L1 adipogenesis in 2D are of limited culture duration (≤15 days), with lipid accumulation manifesting as small lipid droplets (Sheng et al., 2014; Neal and Clipstone, 2002; Sharma et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2013; Pazienza et al., 2016; Bogan et al., 2001; Park et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A multilocular phenotype can signify adipocyte browning, indicating the presence of beige or brown fat.
source: A multilocular phenotype can signify adipocyte browning, indicating the presence of beige or brown fat (Jung et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DFAT cells have been reported to proliferate and accumulate lipids for at least 50 passages while maintaining expression of adipocyte-specific genes such as PPARγ.
source: In this study, porcine dedifferentiated fat (DFAT) cells were used as adipocytes as they been reported to proliferate and accumulate lipids for at least 50 passages while maintaining expression of adipocyte-specific genes such as PPARγ (Nobusue and Kano, 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Intralipid supplementation appeared to rescue 18:2 and 18:3 levels of in vitro porcine adipocytes.
source: Intralipid supplementation appeared to rescue 18:2 and 18:3 levels (while also decreasing 20:1) of in vitro porcine adipocytes, but supplementation also caused FA levels to deviate from native pig fat in other ways (e.g., 15:0, 16:1, 20:3, 20:4, 22:4).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomics data.

claim: In vitro and in vivo porcine adipocytes share similar ratios of MUFAs, PUFAs, and SFAs.
source: When looking at FA saturation however, in vitro and in vivo porcine adipocytes appear to share similar ratios of MUFAs, PUFAs, and SFAs, with Intralipid treatment generally improving the similarity of in vitro and native fats (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by lipidomics data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Lipid supplementation greatly increased primary porcine adipocyte lipid accumulation.
source: When exploring the effects of Intralipid on primary porcine adipocytes, we observed that lipid supplementation greatly increased their lipid accumulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: This approach of aggregating individual adipocytes into a bulk 3D tissue provides a scalable and versatile strategy to produce cultured fat tissue for food-related applications.
source: This approach of aggregating individual adipocytes into a bulk 3D tissue provides a scalable and versatile strategy to produce cultured fat tissue for food-related applications, thereby addressing a key obstacle in cultivated meat production.
evidence: The claim represents the main conclusion of the study based on the experimental findings.
